text: Raissa M. D'Souza is the Associate Dean of Research for the College of Engineering and a Professor of Computer Science and Mechanical Engineering at the University of California, Davis, and serves as an External Professor and member of the Science Board at the Santa Fe Institute. She was elected a Fellow of the American Physical Society in 2016, Fellow of the Network Science Society in 2019, and Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 2024. D'Souza's research focuses on theory and complex systems. When younger, she faced the choice between attending college or moving to Paris to become a fashion designer, ultimately choosing university and studying physics at the University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign. She earned her doctoral degree in theoretical physics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1999, where she worked with Mehran Kardar and Norman Margolus. After graduation, she worked in the fundamental mathematics group at Bell Labs and the Theory group at Microsoft Research, and held visiting research positions at the École Normale Supérieure and the California Institute of Technology. She was appointed Assistant Professor at the University of California, Davis in 2005, promoted to Associate Professor in 2008, and to Full Professor in 2013. Her work centers on the mathematics of networks and the dynamics of processes unfolding on networks, which can exist in technological, biological, or social systems. She has studied node interactions and their role in leading to self-organizing behavior, demonstrating the existence of a percolation threshold where a small number of additional connections can result in a significant fraction of the network becoming connected. This percolation transition applies to various real-world systems, including nanotubes, epileptic seizures, and social networks. Large-scale connectivity and synchronization are essential to the structure and function of complex networks, and she has shown that sparse connections between separate networks can suppress cascading failures. She has also studied cascading behaviors in power-grid failures, financial market crashes, and the spread of political movements. In 2014, D'Souza received a United States Department of Defense Multidisciplinary University Research Initiative Award to investigate the prediction and control of interdependent networks from 2014 to 2019. She is an External Professor at both the Santa Fe Institute and the Complexity Science Hub Vienna, has been a Kavli Fellow of the National Academy of Sciences multiple times, and previously served on the World Economic Forum Global Agenda Council of Complex Systems. She was an inaugural member of the Global Young Academy in 2010. In 2015, she was appointed the 2nd President of the Network Science Society, serving until 2018. In 2019, she received the Network Science Society's inaugural Euler Award "for her influential contribution to the discovery and study of explosive percolation and the insights it provided to explosive synchronization and network optimization." D'Souza serves on the Scientific Advisory Board of Quanta Magazine, was made lead editor of the American Physical Society journal Physical Review Research in 2019, and since August 2020 has been a member of the Board of Reviewing Editors at Science.
